name: Wendy Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential and won't have your name on it. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an underground crew for the electricity company in the city, so no poles for me, it's cables under the streets. We open up the vaults, which are basically concrete rooms under the pavement, pump the water out, and I help the splicer join the cables. He does the clever part, I hand him things, keep things clean and dry, and try to learn by watching.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's steady. Same crew, same yard, same sandwich shop on Mill Street at half eleven. What wears me out is the vaults in summer, it's like an oven down there, and the paperwork on the tablet they gave us last year. I still write things on paper first and copy them in at the end of the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, honestly. Maybe something like, see, all that fuss for nothing. I'm not online much, I don't post, so it'd be a comment in the truck and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, and that's how I like it. I've got a plan: get my splicing ticket, keep saving, buy a place with Tom in a couple of years. I don't need the world to get exciting. I need it to stay boring until we've got the keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep putting money in the house fund, it's about five months of our costs right now, which isn't nothing. Keep working towards the splicing certificate. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you copy notes from paper to the tablet. Why not type them in straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm faster with a pen, and when you're wet and muddy in a vault, the tablet's a pain. The younger guy on our crew, Leo, types everything on the spot and uses some AI thing to write it up. I tried it once, it wrote three paragraphs about a two-line job, so I went back to my notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything in this picture bother you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe that the company spent money on all those AI pilots instead of fixing the pumps in our trucks. But that's management, that's always been a bit like that.

S0.say: I wouldn't say much, maybe that it was all fuss for nothing. I'm not online and I don't post, so it would just be a comment in the truck.
S0.think: It means nothing changes, and that's how I like it. I want to get my splicing ticket, keep saving and buy a place with Tom in a couple of years.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, adding to a house fund worth about five months of costs. Keeps working towards her splicing certificate.
S0.quote: I don't need the world to get exciting. I need it to stay boring until we've got the keys.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy's whole life is pointed at buying a home, and she wants nothing to shake that. She tried an AI tool once and found it wordy and useless, which settled the matter for her. Her mild complaints are about management spending, not about technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, well, it's coming whether we like it or not. At work I'd say let's see what they actually bring in before we all get worked up. I'm not one for marching or petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit worried about the tablet side. If they start putting AI into everything, the planning, the reports, the fault-finding, then the people who are good with that stuff look better than me. I can splice a cable in the dark, eventually. I can't make a tablet like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep saving, but I might push the house back six months to have a bigger cushion. If they made me do an AI course, I'd do it, but I wouldn't go looking for one. I'd mostly wait and see what they actually change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just a bit on edge every time there's a new email from the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tom say about pushing the house back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble. He's a mechanic and his garage already uses a computer to diagnose cars, and he's fine with it, so he'd say I'm overthinking. But he'd go along, he usually does when it's about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one for petitions. Is there anything that would change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they started cutting people, maybe. But I'd want to see it first. I don't like getting angry about things that haven't happened.

S1.say: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's see what they actually bring in before getting worked up. I'm not one for marching or petitions.
S1.think: I'd worry about the tablet side, because if AI goes into planning and reports, people who are good with it look better than me. I can splice a cable, but I can't make a tablet like me.
S1.do: Keeps working and saving, and pushes the house purchase back about six months for a bigger cushion. Does any required AI course without seeking one out, and waits to see what changes.
S1.feel: Uneasy, on edge every time a new email arrives from the office.
S1.quote: I can splice a cable in the dark, eventually. I can't make a tablet like me.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry isn't robots taking the cable work but software changing who looks good at work. She'd delay the house rather than change herself, which is very much her style. Her partner is comfortable with computers in his garage, and she knows he'd think she's overthinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, honestly. Two years? Nobody's ready for that, not the company, not the government, not me. I'd say it in the truck and to my mum, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be in real trouble. I won't even have my splicing ticket in two years, so I'd be a helper in a job that robots are about to do, with no other skills. Everything I've planned is about being steady, and this is the opposite of steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house plan, full stop, and keep the deposit as our emergency money. I'd cut back on everything, no holidays, no takeaways, Tom and I would cook at home. I'd stay at the company as long as they'd keep me, because I don't know what else I'd do, and I'd ask my mum if we could move in with her if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground's gone soft under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum, the first time you talked about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to worry, then I'd sit in her kitchen and worry with her. She runs a little dry cleaner on the corner, she's been doing it for twenty years. If robots can do my job, I don't see why they can't do hers too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at other kinds of work, even outside the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, but I don't know what. Everything I'd think of, a robot could probably do too in this picture. I'd rather hold onto what I've got and hope the company keeps people for safety reasons.

S2.say: I'd say two years is mad and nobody's ready for that, not the company, the government or me. I'd say it in the truck and to my mum, not online.
S2.think: I'd be in real trouble, still a helper without my splicing ticket when robots arrive. Everything I've planned is about being steady, and this is the opposite of steady.
S2.do: Stops the house plan and keeps the deposit as emergency money. Cuts out holidays and takeaways, stays with the company as long as possible and would ask to move in with her mother if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed, as if the ground had gone soft.
S2.quote: Everything I've planned is about being steady, and this is the opposite of steady.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture undoes everything Wendy has organised her life around, the steady job and the house. She has no appetite for a new path and can't see one anyway, so she'd hold tight and lean on family. Her mother's small dry cleaning shop makes the threat feel like it reaches the whole family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's something. At work I'd say let's see what the company plans to do, they must have some idea. I'd keep it practical, not dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd get my splicing ticket, so I'd have a proper trade, at least for a while. I think underground work in old city vaults would be one of the last bits robots can do, because every vault is different and full of water and junk. But it'd still end, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the house for a year or two to see how fast things move. I'd keep saving and work hard to get the splicing ticket early. I wouldn't do much else straight away, I'd wait to see what the first robots actually look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a slower squeeze, but it's still a squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said every vault is different. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month we opened one on the old market square and there were three different kinds of cable down there from three different decades. One had paper insulation, wrapped in lead, from before my mum was born. If a robot can figure that out on its own, fair play, but I'd want to watch it try first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop waiting and do something different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw robots actually doing splicing on a crew somewhere. Not on a video, on a real crew. Then I'd probably start looking at what else I could do, maybe with Tom's garage, but I'd hate it.

S3.say: I'd say five years isn't long but it's something, so let's see what the company plans. I'd keep it practical, not dramatic.
S3.think: Five years means I'd get my splicing ticket and a proper trade for a while. I think old city vaults would be one of the last places robots can manage, but it'd still end, just later.
S3.do: Holds off on buying a house for a year or two to see how fast things move. Keeps saving, pushes to get her splicing ticket early and waits to see the first real robots before doing more.
S3.feel: Anxious, a slower squeeze but still a squeeze.
S3.quote: If a robot can figure that out on its own, fair play, but I'd want to watch it try first.
S3.fieldNote: She takes comfort in how messy old city vaults are, a very concrete reason to think her niche lasts longer. Her trigger for action is seeing a robot on a real crew, not in a video. The house plan again works as her pressure valve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the company and the government to sort it out, so they'd better. At work I'd probably say it'll be the next lot of apprentices who have to worry, not us. Half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me feel a lot better. I'd have my ticket, I'd have years on the job, and we could buy the house sooner rather than later and have most of a decade of paying it off while I've still got work. I don't think about what happens after that, honestly, it's too far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house on the normal plan, in a couple of years, maybe a bit smaller and cheaper than we wanted, so the mortgage is easier if things go wrong. I'd keep saving after that. I'd keep doing my job and see how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's far enough off that I can mostly put it out of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a smaller house. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've been looking at three-bedroom places on the edge of the city. I'd go for a two-bedroom flat nearer the yard instead, so I could cycle in and we'd save on petrol. Tom wants a garage to tinker in. I'd tell him the garage is a ten-year luxury now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't think about after the ten years. Is that true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. Sometimes I think, what if I'm thirty-seven with a mortgage and no job? Then I make a cup of tea and do something else. I'm not someone who plans that far ahead.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the company and government to sort it out, so they'd better. At work I'd joke that it's the next lot of apprentices who should worry.
S4.think: Ten years makes me feel a lot better: I'd have my ticket and years on the job, and we could buy the house soon. I don't really think about what happens after that.
S4.do: Buys a house on the usual timeline, choosing a smaller, cheaper flat near the yard so the mortgage is easier if work dries up. Keeps saving and keeps working as normal.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but far enough off to mostly put out of her mind.
S4.quote: Tom wants a garage to tinker in. I'd tell him the garage is a ten-year luxury now.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Wendy goes back to her plan and simply shrinks it to be safe. She admits she pushes the long-term question away with a cup of tea, which fits her dislike of planning far ahead. The garage her partner wants becomes her symbol of what they'd give up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no ticket and no plan B. What would help is the company promising to keep people on as long as it can and helping us get qualified fast. I don't want a handout, I want the next five years to look like the last five.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how much of this people actually believe. Most people I know don't think robots are coming into vaults any time soon. I'm in the middle, I think it'll come but slower than the people selling it say.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want the next five years to look like the last five.
portrait: Wendy is a 27-year-old helper on an underground cable crew in the city, learning to splice by watching and still writing her notes on paper before typing them up. She doesn't use AI tools and wants life to stay steady until she and her partner Tom can buy a home. She is calm about the plateau, uneasy about software changing who looks good at work, and alarmed by the two-year AGI picture, which would leave her unqualified with no plan B. Her answer to every scenario runs through the house: delay it, drop it or buy smaller. More warning time helps her a lot, mostly because she can put the problem out of her mind.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she would have no splicing ticket and no plan B.
whatWouldHelp: The company promising to keep people on as long as possible and helping workers qualify quickly.
